title: Notes, strings & frets
explanation: There are 12 notes total (A, A#, B, C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#) before they repeat higher. Each fret moves one note up. Open strings are E A D G B E from thickest to thinnest.
fretboardExample: Low E string: open=E, fret1=F, fret2=F#, fret3=G...

quiz.q: What note is the 3rd fret of the low E string?

title: Whole steps, half steps, sharps & flats
explanation: A half step is one fret. A whole step is two frets. A sharp (#) raises a note one half step; a flat (b) lowers it one half step — F# and Gb are the same pitch.
fretboardExample: E to F is a half step (1 fret). E to F# is a whole step (2 frets).

quiz.q: How many frets is a whole step?

title: The major scale
explanation: The major scale follows the pattern Whole-Whole-Half-Whole-Whole-Whole-Half. Starting on C with no sharps/flats gives C D E F G A B C — the 'white keys' scale.
fretboardExample: C major scale on the A string: C(3rd fret) D(5th) E(7th) F(8th) G(10th) A(12th) B(14th) C(15th)

quiz.q: What is the major scale step pattern?

title: Intervals
explanation: An interval is the distance between two notes, e.g. a major 3rd (4 half steps) or a perfect 5th (7 half steps). Chords are built by stacking intervals.
fretboardExample: Root + 7 frets on the same string = a perfect 5th.

quiz.q: How many half steps is a perfect 5th?

title: Chords & triads
explanation: A triad is the simplest chord: root, 3rd, and 5th of a scale stacked together. A major triad sounds bright/happy; a minor triad (flatted 3rd) sounds darker.
fretboardExample: C major triad = C, E, G.

quiz.q: What makes a triad minor instead of major?

title: Chord progressions & keys
explanation: A key is the set of chords that naturally belong together, built from one major scale. The classic beginner progression I-IV-V-I in the key of G is G-C-D-G.
fretboardExample: Key of G major chords: G Am Bm C D Em F#dim.

quiz.q: In the key of G, what is the 'IV' chord?

title: Time signatures, BPM, rhythm & measures
explanation: The top number of a time signature is beats per measure, the bottom is which note value counts as one beat. 4/4 (common time) means 4 quarter-note beats per measure. BPM is how many beats occur per minute.
fretboardExample: In 4/4 at 80 BPM: count '1 2 3 4' evenly, 80 times per minute.

quiz.q: In 3/4 time, how many beats are in each measure?

title: The CAGED system
explanation: CAGED uses the 5 open chord shapes (C, A, G, E, D) as movable barre-chord templates that cover the entire neck for any chord.
fretboardExample: An F barre chord is really an 'E shape' moved up one fret.

quiz.q: F barre chord (root fret 1) uses which open-chord shape?

title: The minor pentatonic scale
explanation: 5 notes per octave, no half-step clashes, making it very forgiving for improvising. It's the most common scale for beginner lead guitar and blues/rock solos.
fretboardExample: A minor pentatonic, box 1: frets 5-8 across all 6 strings starting on the low E's 5th fret.

quiz.q: How many notes are in a pentatonic scale?

title: Seventh chords
explanation: A 7th chord adds a 4th note (the 7th of the scale) on top of a triad, adding tension/color — common in blues, jazz, and pop turnarounds.

quiz.q: What does adding a 7th to a triad do?

title: The Nashville number system
explanation: Chords are written as scale-degree numbers (1, 4, 5, 6m...) instead of letter names, so a progression can be instantly transposed to any key.
fretboardExample: 1-4-5-1 in G = G-C-D-G; the same 1-4-5-1 in C = C-F-G-C.
